title: Symmetric Matrices and the Spectral Theorem
intro: A symmetric matrix is the friendliest kind there is: its eigenvalues are real, its eigenvectors are perpendicular, and it is a sum of simple stretches along perpendicular axes. This page shows why, builds the decomposition for a small example, and then uses it to read off the shape of ellipses and the sign of a quadratic form.

blocks.text: Why symmetric matrices are everywhere

A matrix is symmetric when it equals its own transpose, $A^{\top} = A$: the entry in row $i$, column $j$ equals the entry in row $j$, column $i$. The picture is a mirror along the main diagonal. That sounds like a narrow condition, but a surprising number of the matrices that science and engineering produce have it, for a reason each time.

items: A covariance matrix (see Covariance and Correlation (#/probability/multivariate/covariance-and-correlation)) has entry $\operatorname{cov}(X_i, X_j)$, and covariance does not care which variable is named first.

A stiffness matrix for masses and springs: the force that mass 1 feels per unit move of mass 2 equals the force mass 2 feels per unit move of mass 1. The three-mass example on this page is of that kind, and Eigenvalues in Practice (#/math/eigenvalues/applications) turns it into vibration frequencies.
An inertia tensor in mechanics, which says how hard a body is to spin about each axis.

A Hessian, the matrix of second derivatives of a function of several variables. It is symmetric because mixed partial derivatives do not depend on the order, and its eigenvalues tell you whether a critical point is a valley, a hilltop or a saddle.
$B^{\top}B$ for any matrix $B$, which is always symmetric. It is the starting point of the singular value decomposition, mentioned below.

blocks.text: In every case the eigenvalues turn out to be real numbers with physical meaning (variances, squared frequencies, curvatures), and the eigenvectors turn out to be perpendicular directions with physical meaning too (principal components, modes, principal axes). That is not luck. It is a theorem, and it is short enough to prove here.
The eigenvalues are real

Take the general $2 \times 2$ symmetric matrix with entries $a$, $b$, $d$. Its characteristic polynomial, from Finding Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors (#/math/eigenvalues/finding-eigenvalues), is $\lambda^2 - (a + d)\lambda + (ad - b^2)$, and the quantity under the square root in the quadratic formula is

A sum of two squares cannot be negative, so the square root is real and both roots are real. For $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ it is $0 + 4 = 4$ and the roots are $(4 \pm 2)/2 = 3$ and $1$. Compare a matrix that is not symmetric, such as $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. For a general $2 \times 2$ matrix with entries $a, b, c, d$ the expression is $(a - d)^2 + 4bc$, and here $bc = -1$ so it equals $-4$: the roots are complex (the next page, Complex Eigenvalues and Rotation (#/math/eigenvalues/complex-eigenvalues), is about exactly that).

The argument for any size goes like this. Let $A$ be real and symmetric and suppose $Av = \lambda v$ with $v \ne 0$, where for a moment we allow $v$ and $\lambda$ to be complex. Write $v^{*}$ for the conjugate transpose of $v$ (flip the vector to a row and conjugate each entry). Then $v^{*}Av = \lambda\, v^{*}v$. Now $v^{*}v$ is the sum of $|v_i|^2$, a positive real number. And $v^{*}Av$ is also real: taking its conjugate transpose gives $v^{*}A^{*}v = v^{*}Av$, because a real symmetric $A$ equals its own conjugate transpose, and a number equal to its own conjugate is real. So $\lambda$ is a real number divided by a positive real number: real.
The eigenvectors are perpendicular
Suppose $Av_1 = \lambda_1 v_1$ and $Av_2 = \lambda_2 v_2$ with $\lambda_1 \ne \lambda_2$. Compute the single number $v_1^{\top}Av_2$ in two ways. First, replace $Av_2$ by $\lambda_2 v_2$:

Second, move $A$ to the other side of the product. The transpose of a product reverses the order, so $v_1^{\top}A = (A^{\top}v_1)^{\top} = (Av_1)^{\top}$ because $A^{\top} = A$. This is the one place where symmetry is used. Then replace $Av_1$ by $\lambda_1 v_1$:

The two results are the same number, so $(\lambda_1 - \lambda_2)\, v_1^{\top}v_2 = 0$. The eigenvalues differ, so the dot product $v_1^{\top}v_2$ must be zero: the eigenvectors are perpendicular. Check on the example: $(1, 1) \cdot (1, -1) = 1 - 1 = 0$. If an eigenvalue is repeated the argument says nothing, but one can still choose perpendicular vectors inside its eigenspace; the projection onto a plane is an example, and Repeated Eigenvalues and Defective Matrices (#/math/eigenvalues/repeated-eigenvalues) explains the repeated case.
The spectral theorem: A = QΛQᵀ

Divide each eigenvector by its length so that it has length 1, and call the results $q_1, q_2, \ldots$. They are perpendicular and have length 1, which is the same as saying that $q_i^{\top}q_j$ is 1 when $i = j$ and 0 otherwise. Put them into the columns of a matrix $Q$. Then $Q^{\top}Q = I$, which says $Q^{\top} = Q^{-1}$: the inverse is just the transpose, no calculation needed. A matrix like that is called orthogonal. It turns or flips space without stretching it. The statement 'every real symmetric matrix can be built this way' is the spectral theorem:

This is the diagonalisation $A = PDP^{-1}$ of Diagonalisation and Powers (#/math/eigenvalues/diagonalisation) with a bonus: because $P = Q$ is orthogonal, $P^{-1}$ costs nothing. Worked for the matrix we have been using, the unit eigenvectors are $q_1 = (1, 1)/\sqrt{2}$ for $\lambda_1 = 3$ and $q_2 = (1, -1)/\sqrt{2}$ for $\lambda_2 = 1$ (dividing by $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$ because $|(1, 1)| = \sqrt{2}$). So

Here $Q$ happens to equal its own transpose, which is a coincidence of this example. Multiply out the right-hand side as a check: $\Lambda Q^{\top}$ has rows $3(1, 1)/\sqrt{2}$ and $1(1, -1)/\sqrt{2}$, and then $Q$ times it gives, in the top left, $\tfrac{1}{2}(3 + 1) = 2$, and in the top right $\tfrac{1}{2}(3 - 1) = 1$. The other two entries follow in the same way, giving back $A$.
A sum of projections
There is a second way to read $Q\Lambda Q^{\top}$ that is often more useful. Multiply column by column and you get a sum of one-direction pieces:

blocks.tex: A = \lambda_1\, q_1 q_1^{\top} + \lambda_2\, q_2 q_2^{\top} + \cdots + \lambda_n\, q_n q_n^{\top}

blocks.text: The matrix $q q^{\top}$ is a column times a row: it takes a vector $x$ to $q\,(q^{\top}x)$, which is the part of $x$ along $q$ (the projection, because $q^{\top}x$ is the dot product with a unit vector). So $A$ does this: split $x$ into its parts along the perpendicular axes, stretch the first part by $\lambda_1$, the second by $\lambda_2$, and add them up. For our example:

Apply it to $x = (1, 0)$: the part along $q_1$ is $(0.5, 0.5)$ and along $q_2$ is $(0.5, -0.5)$. Stretch them to $(1.5, 1.5)$ and $(0.5, -0.5)$ and add: $(2, 1)$, which is the first column of $A$, as it must be. Dropping the small terms is the idea behind compressing data: keep the pieces with the largest $|\lambda_i|$ and you have the best low-rank approximation of $A$.
The picture: a circle becomes an ellipse

Put the unit circle through $A$. Every point $x = c_1 q_1 + c_2 q_2$ goes to $\lambda_1 c_1 q_1 + \lambda_2 c_2 q_2$: the coordinates along the perpendicular axes are stretched separately. A circle stretched by different amounts along two perpendicular axes is an ellipse whose axes lie along $q_1$ and $q_2$, with half-lengths $|\lambda_1|$ and $|\lambda_2|$. In the viewer, the green ellipse is that image.

widget.title: Symmetric: the ellipse follows the eigenvectors

params.label: Matrix A
options: your own (use the sliders a, b, c, d)

blocks.text: The preset is $[[2, 1], [1, 2]]$. Look at the green ellipse: its long axis lies along the blue dashed line at 45° and reaches out to 3, its short axis lies along the teal line and reaches 1, and the two lines are at a right angle. Press Sweep v and watch Av: it is longest when v is on the blue line and shortest when v is on the teal line. In the top-right panel, the 'along' curve is $2 + \sin 2\theta$: it touches 3 at 45° and 1 at 135°, and the sideways curve crosses zero at both. At 20° the readout says Av = (2.22, 1.62), length 2.752, turned 16.2°.

This is special to symmetric matrices. For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ the eigenvalues are 5 and 2 along $(1, 1)$ and $(1, -2)$, which are not perpendicular (their dot product is $1 - 2 = -1$; they are 71.6° apart, the viewer prints that). The image of the circle is still an ellipse, but its axes are not along the eigenvectors. The directions that do give the axes come from a different decomposition, the singular value decomposition $A = U\Sigma V^{\top}$, which every matrix has. The longest arrow $Av$ in this example has length 5.117, not 5, and it comes from $v$ at 31.7°, while that longest $Av$, the long axis of the ellipse, points at 39.8° rather than at the eigenvector's 45°. Their half-lengths 5.117 and 1.954 are the singular values, not the eigenvalues 5 and 2. For a symmetric matrix the singular values are the $|\lambda_i|$ and the two decompositions agree.

params.label: Matrix A
options: your own (use the sliders a, b, c, d)

blocks.text: The preset is $[[4, 1], [2, 3]]$ with v at 32°. The readout says the length of Av is 5.117, the largest it ever gets (try 20° for 5.026 and 45° for exactly 5, the eigenvalue). Av at 32° points about 8° further round than v. The two dashed eigen-lines are 71.6° apart, not 90°, and the long axis of the green ellipse does not lie on the blue line.
Quadratic forms and the other ellipse
A symmetric matrix also gives a function of $x$: the quadratic form $x^{\top}Ax$, a single number. For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ and $x = (x_1, x_2)$ it works out as

(The off-diagonal entries each contribute $x_1x_2$, which is why the cross term is $2x_1x_2$.) Substitute $x = c_1 q_1 + c_2 q_2$ and the perpendicular axes decouple everything: $x^{\top}Ax = \lambda_1 c_1^2 + \lambda_2 c_2^2 = 3c_1^2 + c_2^2$. The cross term disappears when you measure along the eigenvectors, and that is the principal-axes theorem. The curve $x^{\top}Ax = 1$ is therefore $3c_1^2 + c_2^2 = 1$, an ellipse with half-axes $1/\sqrt{3} = 0.577$ along $q_1$ and $1/\sqrt{1} = 1$ along $q_2$.

Notice the difference from the picture above. The image of the unit circle has half-axes $\lambda_i$ (3 and 1); the curve $x^{\top}Ax = 1$ has half-axes $1/\sqrt{\lambda_i}$ (0.577 and 1). The same axes, but inverted roles: the large eigenvalue gives the long axis of the image and the short axis of the level curve. Quadratic forms rise fastest in the direction of the largest eigenvalue, so the level curve is pinched there. The viewer draws the image, not the level curve.
Positive definite matrices

A symmetric matrix is positive definite when $x^{\top}Ax > 0$ for every $x \ne 0$. By the decoupling above, $x^{\top}Ax = \lambda_1 c_1^2 + \lambda_2 c_2^2$ with the $c_i$ arbitrary, which is positive for all $c \ne 0$ exactly when every $\lambda_i > 0$. So the test is: all eigenvalues positive. The level curve $x^{\top}Ax = 1$ is then an ellipse (a closed curve), a contour line of a bowl-shaped graph. If one eigenvalue is positive and the other negative, the curve is a hyperbola and the function has a saddle; if one is zero the form is flat along that axis. Positive semidefinite means all $\lambda_i \ge 0$. For $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ the eigenvalues are 3 and $-1$, so it is not positive definite even though its diagonal entries are positive: $x = (1, -1)$ gives $1 - 4 + 1 = -2$.
The Rayleigh quotient

Divide the quadratic form by the squared length of $x$ and you get the Rayleigh quotient $R(x) = x^{\top}Ax / x^{\top}x$. For a unit vector $v$ this is just $v^{\top}Av = v \cdot Av$, the 'along' part of $Av$ that the sweep panel plots. In eigenvector coordinates $R = (\lambda_1 c_1^2 + \lambda_2 c_2^2)/(c_1^2 + c_2^2)$, an average of the eigenvalues weighted by $c_i^2$. An average lies between its extremes, so

with equality at the eigenvectors. This is why the top-right 'along' curve for the symmetric preset oscillates between exactly 1 and 3. For a non-symmetric matrix the along curve is the quadratic form of the symmetric part $(A + A^{\top})/2$ and need not stay between the eigenvalues. The Rayleigh quotient is also how one improves an estimate of an eigenvalue from an estimate of its vector; Power Iteration and Markov Chains (#/math/eigenvalues/power-iteration) uses it.
In three dimensions

The space viewer shows the same story with three perpendicular axes. For a symmetric matrix the green surface is an ellipsoid and the three dashed eigen-lines are its axes. The covariance preset is a symmetric matrix of a cloud of data: the long axis of the ellipsoid points along the direction in which the data spread most.

blocks.text: The preset is $[[3, 1.5, 0.5], [1.5, 2, 0.3], [0.5, 0.3, 0.6]]$. The numbers panel reads $\lambda = 4.176$ along (0.80, 0.58, 0.16), $\lambda = 0.924$ along (−0.56, 0.82, −0.11) and $\lambda = 0.5$ along (−0.20, 0.00, 0.98), and says 'symmetric: real λs, perpendicular eigenvectors'. All three are positive, so the matrix is positive definite, as every genuine covariance matrix must be (positive semidefinite at least). The trace is 5.6, equal to $4.176 + 0.924 + 0.5$: the total variance is shared out among the three axes, and the first axis carries $4.176/5.6 = 75\%$ of it. Drag the view round with the mouse or the Turn and Tilt sliders to see the ellipsoid from the long axis.

widget.title: Masses on springs: the same shapes, a different meaning

params.label: Matrix A
options: cyclic shift (x, y, z) → (z, x, y)
projection onto the plane x + y + z = 0

blocks.text: The matrix $[[2, -1, 0], [-1, 2, -1], [0, -1, 2]]$ is the stiffness matrix of three equal masses joined by springs. Its eigenvalues are $2 + \sqrt{2} = 3.414$, $2$ and $2 - \sqrt{2} = 0.586$, with vectors (−0.50, 0.71, −0.50), (0.71, 0.00, −0.71) and (0.50, 0.71, 0.50) in the numbers panel (the sign of each vector is only a convention). Each vector is a pattern of motion (a mode) in which all three masses swing at one shared frequency, and the eigenvalue sets that frequency ($\omega^2 = \lambda k/m$ for springs of stiffness $k$ and masses $m$); Eigenvalues in Practice (#/math/eigenvalues/applications) works this through. The viewer's walk-through step 5, Next step ▶ five times, says the half-lengths of the ellipsoid axes are these eigenvalues.

For the multivariate normal distribution of The Multivariate Normal (#/probability/multivariate/multivariate-normal) the same decomposition says that the contours of equal density are ellipsoids whose axes are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, with lengths proportional to $\sqrt{\lambda_i}$. For matrices with complex entries, the same theorem holds with Hermitian in place of symmetric; Linear Algebra for Quantum Mechanics (#/quantum/foundations/linear-algebra) and the quantum shelf's Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors (#/quantum/foundations/eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors) use it.
Practice

blocks.title: Spectral decomposition
blocks.text: Find the eigenvalues and unit eigenvectors of $A = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ and write $A$ as a sum of projections.
solution: For $\lambda = 6$: $(A - 6I)v = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4 \end{pmatrix} v = 0$, so $-v_1 + 2v_2 = 0$ and $v = (2, 1)$. Its length is $\sqrt{5}$, so $q_1 = (2, 1)/\sqrt{5}$. For $\lambda = 1$: $\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} v = 0$ gives $2v_1 + v_2 = 0$, $v = (1, -2)$ and $q_2 = (1, -2)/\sqrt{5}$. As expected $(2, 1) \cdot (1, -2) = 0$.

$q_1 q_1^{\top} = \tfrac{1}{5}\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $q_2 q_2^{\top} = \tfrac{1}{5}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}$. Then $6 q_1 q_1^{\top} + q_2 q_2^{\top} = \tfrac{1}{5}\begin{pmatrix} 24 + 1 & 12 - 2 \\ 12 - 2 & 6 + 4 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$, which is $A$.

blocks.title: Is it positive definite?
blocks.text: Decide whether $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ is positive definite. Find a vector that proves your answer, and describe the curve $x^{\top}Ax = 1$.
solution: Trace 4 and determinant $4 - 9 = -5$. The eigenvalues satisfy $\lambda^2 - 4\lambda - 5 = (\lambda - 5)(\lambda + 1) = 0$, so $\lambda = 5$ and $-1$. One is negative, so $A$ is not positive definite.
The eigenvector for $-1$ is $(1, -1)$ (check: $A(1, -1) = (-1, 1)$). The form there is $x^{\top}Ax = (1, -1) \cdot (-1, 1) = -2 < 0$.
In eigen-coordinates $x^{\top}Ax = 5c_1^2 - c_2^2$, so $x^{\top}Ax = 1$ is a hyperbola, not an ellipse.
blocks.answer: No: $\lambda = 5, -1$; the form is $-2$ at $(1, -1)$; the curve is a hyperbola.

blocks.title: The two ellipses
blocks.text: For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ (eigenvalues 6 and 1), give the half-axes of (a) the image of the unit circle and (b) the curve $x^{\top}Ax = 1$, and say which directions they lie along.
solution: Both ellipses have their axes along the eigenvectors $(2, 1)$ and $(1, -2)$, since $A$ is symmetric.
(a) The image has half-axes $|\lambda_i|$: 6 along $(2, 1)$ and 1 along $(1, -2)$.
(b) The level curve has half-axes $1/\sqrt{\lambda_i}$: $1/\sqrt{6} = 0.408$ along $(2, 1)$ and 1 along $(1, -2)$. The long axis of the image is the short axis of the level curve.
blocks.answer: (a) 6 and 1; (b) 0.408 and 1; same directions, roles of long and short swapped.

blocks.title: Rayleigh bounds
blocks.text: For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ compute $v^{\top}Av$ for $v = (1, 0)$ and for $v = (0.6, 0.8)$. Check each against the bounds 1 and 3.
solution: Both lie in $[1, 3]$. The second is close to 3 because $(0.6, 0.8)$ is near the 45° direction of $q_1$. Check with the formula $2 + \sin 2\theta$: $\theta = 53.13°$, $\sin 106.26° = 0.96$, giving 2.96.
